name: Carlos Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollybrook, which is a co-operative farm, so the members own it together and I'm one of the newer members. We've got about six hundred ewes, potatoes and winter wheat. Most days I'm with Marta, the head shepherd, checking ewes, doing feet, moving flocks with the quad bike. In autumn I'm on the potato harvester sorting stones off the belt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's ours, sort of. At the members' meeting my vote counts the same as Marta's, even though she's forgotten more about sheep than I'll ever know. The hard part is I'm still slow, especially at lambing, and I get things wrong that Marta spots from across a field. I sometimes ask one of those AI chat apps what's wrong with a ewe before I ring her, so I don't look daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief and a bit of a joke, honestly. All that money poured into chatbots and they mostly help you write emails. I'd say it at the co-op tea break and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays good. Amira's teaching job is steady, I've got about nine months' wages saved and my co-op shares. The only thing I'd miss is the app telling me a ewe probably has foot rot before Marta does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Hollybrook and try to get better at lambing next spring, with Marta watching less. I'd keep putting money into the co-op shares. Maybe I'd do the sheep shearing course in June, because shearers earn well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Kind of pleased. It means the next ten years look like the last two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI app actually help you with now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little things, like a weird cough. I describe a lame ewe to the AI app and it's right maybe half the time, and Marta's right nearly every time. So it's more for my pride than for the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you at work that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lamb prices, a bit, and the supermarket contract for the potatoes. The buyer squeezed us hard last year and the members argued about it for weeks. But the co-op has money in the bank, so it's not keeping me up.

say: I'd call it a **relief** and a joke at the co-op **tea break**.
I'd say all that money went into chatbots that mostly **write emails**.
think: My life stays good, with **Amira's teaching job**, nine months saved and co-op shares.
The real pressure is the **supermarket buyer** squeezing our potato price, not AI.
do: Keep working the **ewes** at Hollybrook and get better at **lambing** next spring.
Book the **shearing course** in June because shearers earn well.
feel: **Calm** and pleased that the next ten years look like the last two.
S0.quote: I describe a lame ewe to the AI app and it's right maybe half the time, and Marta's right nearly every time.
fieldNote: He uses the chat app mostly to **save face** in front of the head shepherd.
His security rests on **three legs**: savings, co-op shares and his partner's job.
He mentions the **supermarket buyer** as the co-op's real enemy, unprompted.

steps.text: Keep working the ewes at Hollybrook and improve at lambing
Book the June sheep shearing course
Add to the co-op member shares each quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should own whatever machines come in, not some lender. If robots save money, the members should share it. I'd say that at the members' meeting and I'd probably post it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my day is mostly hands-on, so the slow robots don't scare me much. The thinking stuff will hit the farm office, where Kath does the orders and the potato contracts. I'd worry for Kath more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI app more seriously, maybe for the flock records, once Marta says it's worth it. I'd push the members to vote for a rule: no member loses work because of a machine. And I'd do the shearing course anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for others. It'd be on my mind every members' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's Kath, and what would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kath runs the office three days a week, all the orders and the paperwork for the subsidies. I'd tell Kath to learn the new software before someone decides the farm office doesn't need her. I'd feel awful saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only use the app more once Marta says so. Why wait for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she's the one who knows sheep, and I've seen tech come in that wasted everyone's time. The co-op bought electronic ear tag readers that nobody used for a year. I'd rather follow once it's proven.

say: I'd say the **co-op** should own any machines, so members share the savings.
I'd raise it at the **members' meeting** and probably post it online too.
think: My day is **hands-on**, so slow-spreading robots don't scare me much.
The office work goes first, so I'd worry more for **Kath** than for myself.
do: Use the AI app for **flock records** once Marta says it's worth it.
Propose a **members' vote** that no member loses work because of a machine.
Finish the **shearing course** to add a skill that pays.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for colleagues like Kath than for himself.
S1.quote: I'd tell Kath to learn the new software before someone decides the farm office doesn't need her.
fieldNote: He reads the scenario well: **office tasks** at the co-op go first, his work later.
He waits for **proof** before adopting tech, citing ear tag readers nobody used.
His politics show up as **co-op ownership** of machines rather than resisting them.

steps.text: Start keeping the flock records with the AI app
Propose a members' vote protecting jobs from machines
Finish the sheep shearing course this summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a law, fast, that shares the gains, like a robot tax that pays people a basic income. I'd join whatever campaign the farm workers' union started. I'd say it everywhere, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI in 2028 runs our office and the potato contracts overnight, and I'd mostly shrug. But robots in 2031 that can lamb and shear, that's my whole job. I'd be thirty-one and not even good at sheep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd use the first three years to get into whatever the co-op needs once robots come, like looking after the machines or the land plans. I'd ask the members to buy robots together, so we own them. I'd keep my savings untouched as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a plan, sort of, but two years is fast and I'm not sure the plan holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Amira the school will need her longer than the farm will need me. Teachers might be safer for a bit, kids still need a person in the room. Then we'd talk about whether I can afford to retrain on her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the co-op really afford robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. We'd have to borrow, and members would fight about it. But the alternative is the big farm next door buys them and undercuts our lamb price, so I'd argue we have no choice.

say: I'd call for a **robot tax** that pays everyone a basic income.
I'd join the farm workers' **union campaign**, because two years is nothing.
think: AI running the office in **2028** I'd shrug at, but **robots in 2031** take my job.
I'd be thirty-one and **not even good** at sheep yet.
do: Ask the members to **buy robots together** so the co-op owns them.
Train into **machine upkeep** or land planning before 2031.
Keep my **savings** untouched as a buffer.
feel: **Anxious**, with half a plan and doubts it will hold.
S2.quote: I'd tell Amira the school will need her longer than the farm will need me.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** deliberately, to retrain before robots arrive.
He wants the co-op to **own the robots**, partly so a bigger farm doesn't undercut them.
He leans on **Amira's job** as the household's safer income.

steps.text: Ask Hollybrook members to buy robots together
Train in farm robot upkeep before 2031
Join the farm workers' union campaign for a robot tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set this up fairly, so let's not waste them. The co-op should be the model: workers own the machines. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years helps me more than most. It's enough to learn the robot side properly and still be under forty when the robots hit in 2034. Kath and the office get hit in 2031 though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a farm machinery course at the agricultural college, evenings, within the year. I'd keep my shares and maybe buy more. I'd still keep shepherding, because I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. I'd have something to work toward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would that course cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand for the year, I think, and the co-op might pay half. I'd pay the rest out of savings without blinking. That's what savings are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say five years helps you. What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots might fix themselves, honestly. Self-repairing robots could mean I've trained for a job that's also shrinking. I try not to think about that bit.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to set this up fairly, so don't waste them.
The **co-op** should be the model, with workers owning the machines.
think: Five years lets me learn the **robot side** and still be under forty in 2034.
The **office staff** get hit first, in 2031, before my hands-on work.
do: Start an **evening machinery course** at the agricultural college within the year.
Pay about **£1,000** from savings if the co-op covers half.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because there's something to work toward.
S3.quote: Self-repairing robots could mean I've trained for a job that's also shrinking.
fieldNote: Five years turns his **half-plan** into a real course with a cost.
He spots the weak point himself: **robot upkeep** jobs may shrink too.
He'd still keep **shepherding** while training, out of love for the work.

steps.text: Enrol on an evening farm machinery course at the college
Buy more co-op shares from savings
Keep shepherding the Hollybrook ewes while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the chance to do it right: retrain people, share ownership, set rules. If we mess it up with ten years' warning, that's on us. I'd say it at the co-op and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is comfortable for me. I'd be good at sheep by then and probably running the co-op's machines too. As long as the co-op owns the robots, my income should be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the machinery course in a couple of years, not rushing it. I'd learn the AI tools properly once everyone's using them. And I'd stand for the co-op's board, because decisions about robots need people like me in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'd be all right, but it's a big change for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now it's all older members on the board, and they'll retire before 2039. Hollybrook's board will decide which robots we buy and who stays on, so someone my age should be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have a life, honestly. Amira and I want a house, and maybe kids later. Ten years means I don't have to choose between that and retraining.

say: I'd say ten years is the chance to **share ownership** and set rules properly.
If we mess up with **ten years' warning**, the blame is ours.
think: By 2039 I'd be good at sheep and likely **running the machines** too.
If the co-op **owns the robots**, my income should be fine.
do: Take the **machinery course** in a couple of years without rushing.
Stand for the **co-op board**, since it will decide which robots to buy.
Learn the **AI tools** properly once everyone is using them.
feel: **Uneasy**, sure he'll be fine but worried for the people around him.
S4.quote: Hollybrook's board will decide which robots we buy and who stays on, so someone my age should be there.
fieldNote: With a decade, his answer shifts from **retraining** to **gaining power** in the co-op.
He separates his own outlook (fine) from the **community** (worried), which keeps him uneasy.
Ten years lets him plan a **house and family** alongside work.

steps.text: Stand for election to the Hollybrook co-op board
Take the farm machinery course in about two years
Learn the farm AI tools once the co-op adopts them
Save toward a house with Amira

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough for a co-op to agree on anything, never mind buy robots. What would help is cheap loans for co-ops to buy machines together, so the farm keeps the savings and not a big company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the robots. That's the whole question for me. A robot owned by the people who used to do the work is a holiday, and a robot owned by someone else is a redundancy letter.

headlineQuote: A robot owned by the people who used to do the work is a holiday, and a robot owned by someone else is a redundancy letter.
portrait: Carlos, 27, is a junior **shepherd** and member of Hollybrook, a co-operative farm with six hundred ewes.
He has nine months saved, **co-op shares** and a partner, Amira, who teaches.
He adopts tech **once it's proven** and uses an AI chat app now and then for sick ewes.
His answer to every scenario is **shared ownership**: the co-op should own the robots.
He moves from calm to **anxious** in the fast AGI worlds, and plans to retrain into machinery.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because a co-op can't agree and buy robots in two years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for co-ops to buy machines together, so savings stay with the farm.
